correctness.rationale: In an inclined central plane with coordinates (u cos beta,v,u sin beta), a radial ray has quadratic intersection rho^2-2R sqrt(1-sin^2 beta cos^2 phi) rho+(R^2-r^2)<=0. Because the root product R^2-r^2>0, admissible intervals avoid the origin. For R sin beta<r all angles are allowed (annulus); above this threshold they form two components, each a disk. The area is 2R integral_0^{2pi} sqrt(1-s^2 cos^2 phi) sqrt((r^2-R^2 s^2 cos^2 phi)_+)dphi. It decreases strictly from 4pi Rr to 2pi r^2; at beta*=asin(r/R) the integral evaluates to 4r sqrt(R^2-r^2)+4R^2 asin(r/R). Near each of two degenerate angles, integrating sqrt((r^2 t^2+delta)_+) gives -(delta/(2r))log(|delta|/r^2) plus O(delta), for delta=r^2-R^2 sin^2 beta. Delta=-2Rr sqrt(1-(r/R)^2)(beta-beta*)+O((beta-beta*)^2), yielding the common coefficient 4(R^2-r^2) multiplying (beta-beta*)log|beta-beta*| and derivative tending to minus infinity. A Haar normal has |n_z| uniform, hence beta density sin beta and the topology probabilities; change of variables gives f_A(a)|log(|a-A*|/R^2)| -> (r/R)/(4(R^2-r^2)). Independent high-precision integrals for (R,r)=(2,1),(3,2) recovered area constants and cusp slopes 11.99999987 versus 12, and 19.99999983 versus 20. Full proof is local analytic, not a numerical extrapolation.
